entries.title: The Kindle Accessories I Never Want to Read Without (2026)
entries.summary: Looking to better protect your Kindle or add a little personality to your favorite e-reader? From cases and covers to page-turners and stickers, this is the guide for you.
entries.content:
Your Kindle doesn't have to be just a plain e-reader. The right Kindle accessories can transform the simple device into something that showcases your personality, makes it easier to read, or all of the above. Personally, I'm always looking for a way to hold up one less device in front of my face; I'm holding my phone enough already, thank you very much.

If you're shopping around for new Kindle accessories, I've got you covered as a fellow reader and owner of every single current Kindle model. I've tried everything from clear cases you can fill with stickers to ones with built-in straps, and have tested straps you can add to your e-reader without needing a case. Stickers? Charms? Got ’em. Hate holding your Kindle up to read? The Kindle holders and page-turning remotes are for you. This guide will give you ideas on how to improve your own reading time or gift your favorite reader.

As new Kindle models are rolling out that aren't the same size as the old, it's important to double-check what size and generation Kindle accessory you're getting. Most accessories in this guide were tested on the 2024 generation, unless otherwise noted.

Updated October 2026: I've added notes on the new Kindle Page Turn Case and Kindle Click, plus cases and grips from Bondi.

My Favorite Kindle Accessories

Kindle Cases and Covers

An easy must-have for any Kindle reader is a case or cover to protect your e-reader. Here are some of my favorites that I've tried on my various Kindles.

All of these were tested on 2024 models of the Kindle, usually the 7-inch Paperwhite or Colorsoft. The new 2026 generation has some slight size differences, so if you're shopping for accessories for a newer Kindle, double-check if there's a version for the model you have.

Kindle Straps and Grips

Looking for an easier way to hold your Kindle? Add these straps and grips right onto the Kindle or the case.

Kindle Holders

Hate holding up your Kindle? Or struggle with chronic pain that makes holding it feel terrible? These holders will literally take the weight out of your hands.

A Page Turner Made for Kindle

Page turners have been the latest item to have as an e-reader user, but while Kobo launched a remote last year, Kindle had yet to have one—until now.

Kindle announced the release of the Kindle Click, its first Bluetooth page-turning remote, in early October, and it's finally available to buy. It's a huge improvement over third-party devices that required you to have one part of the device on your Kindle so it could tap and turn the page for you, and a remote in your hand. The worst part was not just that it blocked some of the screen, but that you had to track the battery life of two separate pieces.

The Kindle Click solves these complaints, and while it launched on the same date as the new Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft, it's backward compatible with Kindle models from 2024. It's easy to set up: Just go into your device settings, click on Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and then Bluetooth devices to sync your Kindle Click. I tried it with both a 2024 Kindle and a 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, and both devices were able to find the Click almost instantly and start working.

The Click has two buttons on the main body that move forward and backward and will move around a page you're on, too (but won't select a book for you; it'll just move through your library or homepage). There are also two buttons on the right side that let you adjust screen brightness, which is a fantastic convenience. There's also an included lanyard to attach it to your wrist. It's great to pair with a Kindle stand of any kind so you can prop up your Kindle and turn the page without lifting a finger.

Some Charger Options

If you're getting a new Kindle, you might not be thrilled to discover you need to provide your own charging block to charge it. And if you haven't already switched over your home's collection of wall chargers to USB-C, you'll be especially frustrated when you open the box and find only a USB-C cord. If you're in the market for a new wall charger to pair with your Kindle, these are a couple of our favorites.

Looking to charge on the go? You shouldn't need to with a Kindle's long battery life. But in case you're a serial battery drainer, you can try these portable power banks we love. If neither of these suit you, check out our complete guide to the Best Power Banks.

Kindle Adornments

While everything else in this guide serves a protective or convenience purpose, this section features items with a singular purpose: fun. Here are a few I've liked adding to my Kindle.

Kindle Bags and Sleeves

Looking for a bag to tote your Kindle around? These carriers have you covered with a specific size and special pockets designed to safely store your device. Sure, you could throw your Kindle in any old bag, but these will keep it secure and prevent scratches from your keys. If you'd rather use the bag you have but want a separate sleeve to keep it safe, we've got ideas for that too.

Still Need a Kindle?

If you're reading this guide and actually are still in need of a Kindle, we've got an entire guide to the best Kindles to buy and why. The newest models are (for the most part) the smartest buy, unless the older 2024 models are on sale.

FAQs

Can These Accessories Work With Other E-Readers, Like Kobo?

Some of them can! You'll have to check descriptions for certain items (like cases or things that have to perfectly fit the device) since other devices like Kobo and Nook don't have the same dimensions as a Kindle, but flexible straps, generic tablet holders, and decorative items like charms and stickers would easily work with any other e-reader you own.

entries.title: An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
entries.summary: Anthropic and OpenAI say they’ve disproved a key tenet of computer science. Researchers are struggling with the fall but also feel like “overexcited bunnies” as they look at new questions to explore.
entries.content:
Linköping University professor Peter Jonsson is set to have his work presented in two weeks’ time at one of the most prestigious conferences in theoretical computer science. As of Monday, much of that work is “dead,” he says, after AI showed that a 27-year-old hypothesis underpinning it is wrong.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic claimed this week to have disproved the exponential time hypothesis (ETH). Vast swaths of theoretical computer science research on complexity and algorithm design have been built on the premise that the effort it takes to solve certain problems increases exponentially with the size of the problem.

Jonsson expects his predicament will be “very common” at the IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, where his work will be presented by one of his coauthors. “People will start the talks: ‘ETH is false, half of my paper does not work,’” he says. It’s a vexing problem, Jonsson says, “but at the same time, we learn a lot from it. And this is what science is about.”

Researchers haven’t independently verified, let alone had time to fully understand, the AI-produced proofs, which both firms have published on GitHub in both natural language and its machine-checkable Lean format. OpenAI has asked the UC Santa Barbara computer scientists who originally proposed the hypothesis, plus an MIT academic who has refuted a version of ETH, to rally researchers to unpack the proofs. So far, this effort includes a Google form asking for volunteers and feedback, and a commitment from OpenAI to fund a conference on the topic.

UC Santa Barbara professor Daniel Lokshtanov plans to join the effort, as he estimates the result—if confirmed—will render him “galactically wrong” and make around 50 of his published papers either “pointless” or in need of a revisit.

“It’s just a giant bomb dropped into the middle of the field,” he says. “It’s really cool and terrible at the same time.”

Thore Husfeldt, head of the algorithms research group at the IT University of Copenhagen, had spent most of this year thinking about one single problem in his subfield. “As far as I can tell, it’s now all irrelevant,” he tells WIRED. Having first formulated a version of the hypothesis now disproved by OpenAI, he has been writing calculations on his blackboard to figure out what other parts of his work might have become obsolete due to the “once-in-a-generation result.” Unlike the ennui that has gripped math researchers who have faced similarly field-upending proofs generated by AI models, though, Husfeldt expressed enthusiasm about the new results.

The finding is “fantastic,” he says. “Being a mathematician is a lot like stumbling about in a completely dark room,” he explains. “It's like somebody just illuminated an entire subfield in floodlights of knowledge, and now we just run around like overexcited bunnies and look at all the nooks and crannies that we can suddenly explore. So it’s a super exciting time.”

For centuries, science has advanced through making hypotheses and proving them wrong. It also isn’t unusual for an academic to be scooped or have their work otherwise undercut by another research group. But AI has accelerated this, obliterating whole research programs and spooking researchers in specific fields of math and science who wonder where they stand now that machines can outperform them.

“The last few months have been really tough. It's a lot of doom and gloom, because every week, or every second week, the results announced by AI just annihilate the ongoing research projects of many people,” Husfeldt says. “That is psychologically taxing for many people,” he says, adding that his department has considered hiring an occupational psychologist because “some people are really depressed and really sad.”

Researchers have also been overwhelmed by the volume of content now being produced, thanks to AI, including slop-level results. Midway through the interview, Husfeldt receives what he suspects to be an AI-generated 17-page paper on the consequences of the ETH result from a random Gmail account. He won’t read it: “Reading math is a very big investment of cognitive time,” he says.

OpenAI has directly contributed to this; earlier this month, it dumped 722 manuscripts on 400 problems on GitHub, to the annoyance of academics, who complain this makes it difficult to digest the results. Adding to the frustration were several documents that contained errors, reflecting what some mathematicians saw as a hasty rollout designed to juice the company’s planned initial public offering rather than moving the field forward. This time around, OpenAI’s 60-odd-page paper on ETH seems to be written better than the companies’ past publications, academics tell WIRED.

They are now scrambling to unpack the paper and find what other results they can quickly deduce from it.

If ETH is false and it doesn’t, in fact, take exponentially more time to solve problems as they become more complex, that’s “exciting,” says Victor Lagerkvist, an associate professor at Linköping. He plans to return to problems he had previously given up on under the assumption ETH was accurate.

OpenAI’s finding could also have impacts on the cryptography that underpins web security, which is based on the assumption that certain mathematical problems take an impractically long time to solve. While this particular result doesn’t directly affect cryptography, “it should definitely scare some cryptosystem designers,” says Lokshtanov.

That’s why continued human and AI-assisted work in theoretical computer science is important, Husfeldt adds: “We want the open scientific process to identify our misunderstandings about computation, in particular because lots of modern digital infrastructure is built on assumptions about computation.”

As for Linköping’s Jonsson, he plans to revisit both his own and others’ papers that hinge on ETH being true, and believes his conference paper may eventually be salvageable through another method. He’s excited to look into the details of OpenAI’s proof and see what he can learn from it and apply it to new problems. Even though it undoes the assumptions underpinning his work, having a verdict for ETH is something he could only “dream of” before, he says. “These are exciting times,” he adds. “Most people would never experience anything like this in their career.”

“I don’t care if it's a human-written proof, or it's written by AI, or if an alien transmitted this proof to us. If it’s true, then we must simply use it in the future.’’

entries.title: Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED TV: Midrange Quality, Upscale Color Accuracy
entries.summary: The Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED is more affordable than competitors and offers exceptional color accuracy, but is otherwise just OK.
entries.content:
An array of brilliant colors is what you want from an RGB television, and on that front, the Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED delivers. After having reviewed a number of the top RGB TVs, including the flagship Hisense UR9 RGB MiniLED and offerings from Samsung and LG, I can report that this UR8 is solidly good. It provides mini RGB tech at a lower price than the impressive UR9. As long as you can accept UR8's lacking contrast and brightness capabilities—at least compared to its high-performing sibling—the television's color accuracy stands to wow you.

What makes RGB models like the Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED so interesting is that you can tweak the picture quality for more brilliant and accurate colors. While testing proved the UR9 has a brighter panel that performs at a higher caliber for movies, shows, games, and even displaying artwork, the UR8 is certainly colorful. But are the compromises of this more budget-friendly model worth the savings? That has less of a clear, black-and-white answer.

Setting Up Shop

The UR8 is a bit thicker than the UR9, but it is otherwise visually similar: They appear to have the same chassis and similarly feature a single pedestal. The stand snaps into place and requires some screws, but the assembly process is overall straightforward and quick. Installation couldn't be simpler: Just scan a QR code that connects to Google Home and move through the steps.

The left side of the TV houses all of the port inputs: an Ethernet port for reliable streaming, an optical audio port, a coaxial port, and one USB-A port for external storage or connecting an HD antenna. Like the UR9, this model supports Wi-Fi 6E for speedy and reliable streaming. For color accuracy, the UR8 meets 100 percent of the BT.2020 spec and is Pantone Validated, meaning it can showcase a broad selection of color variation.

entries.title: A Hacker Targeted High-Stakes Poker Players With Malware That Exposed Their Cards
entries.summary: Illicit software on the computers of some of the world’s best online poker players allowed the accused cheater to see what cards were in the victims’ hands—and trounce them at the tables.
entries.content:
In a fitting sign of the times, the hacker’s carefully laid plans were foiled by an AI agent.

It was September 25, 2026, and Alex, a professional online poker player, was using his Claude AI agent to review some play statistics. (Alex only agreed to speak with WIRED under a pseudonym to avoid any risk of reprisals from threat actors.) After Alex’s SQL database crashed and needed to be reset, the Claude agent noticed something suspicious: A program called MeshAgent was operating in the background, where it seemed to be capable of capturing Alex’s screen and even controlling his entire machine.

Thanks to the Claude agent’s report, Alex could see the program had been installed on April 24, and not by Alex himself. Alex says the agent identified 11 time-stamped events when the program had been capturing his screen based on graphic errors it caused during screen sharing instances. During all 11, Alex had been playing a session on ACR, also called Americas Cardroom, a major worldwide online poker operator.

He checked his hand histories and quickly found the most troubling info yet: The same opponent, playing under the handle OxOO, was at his table for 10 of those 11 sessions.

The handle was familiar. Alex and several friends in the high-stakes community had shared suspicions about this player’s behavior in the past. Alex checked the player’s win rate stats via a public tracking site; they were astronomically higher than the best players in the world, a statistical impossibility given the sample of hands played. In Alex’s view, it was glaringly obvious that this player was cheating.

An investigation by Alex and other members of the high-stakes community in subsequent days confirmed his fears—and then some. Alex was one of hundreds of players allegedly targeted with this type of malware by the same reported threat actor across a period of multiple years. Alex, who was the first to discover MeshAgent on his computer, claims he was “only” ripped off for around $30,000, a relatively moderate sum for the level he plays at; many of his peers weren’t so lucky.

With millions of dollars allegedly stolen across the biggest sites on the internet, the poker world is searching for answers about how the scheme was allowed to continue so long, whether major sites took the risk seriously after it was reported, and whether online poker itself has been irreversibly compromised.

Poker has never been short on cheating controversies; online poker especially so. The “superuser” method, in which a cheater gains unauthorized access to their opponents’ cards and can therefore act with perfect information against them, was one of the first to show up online.

Two major sites in online poker’s early days, Absolute Poker and Ultimate Bet, served as cautionary tales in the mid-2000s. In separate instances, superuser cheaters were able to gain insider access to the websites and bilk players for millions of dollars. (Much of the loot was refunded to players following an investigation.) Those high-profile incidents led to tightened security measures from many top poker sites.

Another minor superuser incident took place in 2013, when a Finnish high-stakes player said his laptop had been stolen from his hotel room during a European Poker Tour tournament in Barcelona. When the laptop was recovered, it had been infected with malware that allowed a hacker to view his screen remotely. And maybe the most famous superuser scandal of all took place on the live felt: In a story that made it all the way to SportsCenter, a player named Mike Postle was accused of stealing over $250,000 from livestreamed games at Stones Gambling Hall in 2018 and 2019 with the aid of what observers believed to be an alleged accomplice with access to live card data who fed information to Postle’s phone. (Postle denied the accusations, alleging it was “fake news.”)

Outside one relatively small (and quickly remedied) incident in 2023, though, the online poker world had gone years without a confirmed superuser incident—until now. And some of what’s known about this latest attempt signals a savvier threat actor than in previous scandals, plus a degree of patience not typically seen in attacks like these.

“Traditionally, when you see these types of financially motivated threat actors, they will get access to a system and then as soon as they’re on it, they’ll do a scope of what they have access to and then they’ll hit everyone all at once and dump all the wallets,” says WolfSec, a cybersecurity professional who consults with many high-stakes poker players on security measures. He was first to break the news of the MeshAgent scam on September 29, on his X account. (WolfSec agreed to speak to WIRED under the condition his real name not be used out of fears of reprisals from hackers; WIRED independently confirmed his credentials as a cybersecurity expert.)

But this hacker didn’t do any of that, despite many of these players having large cryptocurrency holdings and other investments accessible on their machines. The attacker seemed instead to be performing advanced reconnaissance. In fact, WolfSec believes the same threat actor was attempting to attack players’ machines as early as 2022 using a more basic technique; because no known funds were stolen at the time, no other action was taken once the players wiped the malware from their computers.

It appears, though, that the hacker was simply biding his time and improving his methods in preparation for an eventual strike.

Instead of targeting individual players directly, this more recent attack involved third-party software programs called IntuitiveTables and Jurojin. These programs allow professionals to play dozens of online poker hands at once. Using these popular “multi-table” tools, players can switch between live games with a keystroke, place bets or make plays with hot keys, and other actions that make it easier to play at several virtual tables at the same time. The hacker compromised both applications, WolfSec says, pushing malicious software to over a thousand estimated users.

In the case of Jurojin, the attacker gained access to the developer’s own system for software updates and was able to deliver the remote-access agent to existing users through normal, automatic updates.

The developer of Intuitive Tables was running Jurojin on their test computer, and that machine got the remote-access agent as part of Jurojin’s compromised software update. Using the agent, the attacker added malicious code to the Intuitive Tables application before the developer signed the security certificate for an updated build of the app. That version carrying the malicious code was posted to the Intuitive Tables website as a public download, and everyone who installed that version of the app unknowingly also installed a backdoor on their computer.

In both instances, the malicious code was delivered through a standard update channel or an official release, so neither the users nor their antivirus apps detected anything amiss.

The modified version of Intuitive Tables behaved exactly like the clean version, with one exception: It also checked players’ files for their usernames.

“If you were on a hard-coded list that was stored on the attacker’s infrastructure, which [the malware] reached out to and downloaded and compared your username to, then it acted as a malicious program and downloaded additional malicious files,” WolfSec says. “If you weren’t on that list, then it became the normal program and didn’t do anything malicious at all.”

The list appears to have been populated primarily with regular high-stakes players across several sites. All of the players on the list appear to have had the MeshAgent program installed covertly on their machines. The hacker was ready to pounce.

In early 2025, a couple of new players began frequenting high-stakes games—one on ACR (using the handle “JackKlompus”) and another major global site called CoinPoker (handle: “Europe”). Strangely, despite not being familiar to other regulars in these games, the players refused to identify themselves in table chats, a common request that’s typically granted by new players in high-stakes poker. The new opponents were also winning with improbable frequency. (Later, once the pros started sharing information about their games, it was pieced together that these players were the same person.)

Mike, a professional poker player who spoke to WIRED using a pseudonym due to fear of reprisals from hackers, played on both sites at the time and was at tables with the player using these handles. Mike says at first he wondered if the mystery player’s success was somehow explainable. Maybe they were doing something new that Mike and his fellow pros just hadn’t figured out.

“You could kind of excuse it” at first, Mike says. “Maybe this guy is really, really good or something.”

As the number of winning hands grew, though, Mike and several high-stakes friends became more suspicious. They initially suspected that the player was using real-time assistance via game-theory-based engines that outperform the best human players. Real-time assistance is banned across major sites, but is difficult to police perfectly and is something pros are regularly watching out for. Mike mostly stopped playing at tables with the mystery player, as a precaution.

Like WolfSec, Mike reflects on a relative level of skill and discipline employed by this player during those 2025 sessions, especially compared to other known cheaters in poker history. The account generally used standard bet sizes and played normal hand ranges. Its session-by-session play never raised too many eyebrows; only the account’s win rate over time drew scrutiny.

But in June 2026, Mike played a two-hour heads-up (one-on-one) session on a different site, ClubWPT Gold, which he’d later determine—following reviews with the website’s security team—came against the same player from the 2025 sessions. The player used a different handle to evade detection, so Mike didn’t see a reason to be extra cautious. The opponent simply steamrolled Mike, making every correct decision even in seemingly impossible spots—almost like he could see Mike’s cards. “It was very blatant,” Mike says.

Immediately after the session, Mike messaged several friends in the high-stakes world to say he thought he’d been cheated.

Turns out he was right. When word of the hack broke publicly on WolfSec’s X account, ClubWPT Gold investigated. The site banned the account Mike had played against and refunded him for his losses, says Randy Lundy, head of customer operations for ClubWPT Gold.

This alleged cheater’s presence in online circles was an open secret across the community by this point. In fact, Mario Mosböck, a poker ambassador for CoinPoker who was authorized to speak about the company’s response to the hack, says the site began investigating this player as early as 2025, banning them and refunding over $100,000 in allegedly stolen funds to affected players. (Mosböck says the return of funds was delayed several months because the alleged cheater appealed the confiscation to regulators.) The player’s simple win rate and play style statistics appeared to be evidence of malfeasance, even if the site couldn’t definitively determine how the cheating was happening.

How, then, was the same alleged cheater allowed to keep ripping off players like Alex and Mike on multiple other supposedly reputable sites more than a year later?

“They confirmed multiple times that they looked at my report, but for whatever reason they didn't act on it,” says Patrick Howard, a professional poker player and founder of the coaching company Mobius Poker.

The “they” he’s referring to is GGPoker, arguably the most well-known site in the world for non-US players. Howard says he submitted a report to the site in early September 2026, weeks before the MeshAgent hack became public, highlighting the alleged cheater’s unusual play and urging the site to investigate.

“I found multiple three- to four-standard-deviation outliers,” Howard says, and that was across a limited hand history sample sent to him by friends and clients. He sent his findings to the GGPoker team but received no response. He got a reply only after WolfSec’s public reveal of the hack on X, with the site telling him there “wasn’t conclusive evidence” to act at the time of his complaint.

Various online poker sites handled the incident differently. Players have largely praised CoinPoker for proactively banning the player based on win rate and play tendencies alone, which are accepted as definitive indicators of cheating at stakes this high and with samples this large; while ClubWPT Gold only seems to have been impacted later in the scheme, that site also appears to have acted decisively upon discovering it.

But the hacker remained active on GGPoker and ACR until late September, allegedly stealing between $1.5 million and $4 million, based on the estimates of the sources WIRED spoke to for this story.

“Players are frustrated, because they had been reporting this for a year,” says John Andress, head of game integrity for A5 Labs, a cybersecurity platform that provides anti-cheating services to ClubWPT Gold and other brands. “A few of the platforms just completely ignored them.”

This was despite signs that many feel were all too obvious.

CoinPoker says the player’s alleged true identity was known early in this process, after the company conducted a webcam security interview with them in February 2025. The name the player gave matched the handle the player later used on GGPoker, which requires players to use their real name as their handle instead of a pseudonym for certain high-stakes games. (WIRED is not naming the player because they have not been charged with any crime. The player did not respond to multiple requests for comment on this story). The CoinPoker spokesman says their team reached out to ACR with their findings as well and received no response. (Requests for comment from WIRED to ACR and GGPoker received no reply.)

To its credit, GGPoker acknowledged the incident and announced several fixes in an October 15 blog post, including banning third-party tools and adding win-rate anomaly detection. The site also says it traced the accused attacker’s funds to a Coinbase account and has asked the crypto company to restrict the account and preserve its records; it says it also provided the wallet addresses to industry watchdogs and law enforcement.

But ACR is going the opposite direction: On October 18, it emailed players claiming its security team found no compromised game outcomes or wrongdoing and will not issue any refunds—despite, in the same email, announcing a new feature to stop remote-viewing tools from capturing the images of the cards in players’ hands.

Other entities have taken concrete action: Both Jurojin and IntuitiveTables (via its Discord channel) released tools to help users detect whether the MeshAgent hack had affected their machines. AceGuardian, a research group that’s part of A5 Labs, put out an open-source “superuser detection” tool designed for use on any poker site. WolfSec says he submitted a complaint to the the Internet Crime Complaint Center, the cybercrime arm of the FBI, and has been working with players on improving machine security. The FBI, when reached for comment by WIRED, would not confirm receipt nor any details of this complaint.

But these efforts will be so successful only if the sites treat these incidents with more scrutiny and don’t just spring into action in the aftermath of major attacks.

“Ultimately, the sites have to ban the players,” Howard says. “I think they dropped the ball here.”

entries.title: I Did Push-Ups With Snap’s Chunky AR Glasses
entries.summary: They fit better than they look and stay put when you move, but Snap’s $2,195 Specs still feel like a developer prototype in search of a purpose.
entries.content:
I hadn’t expected to be doing augmented reality push-ups in the middle of the mall. Yet there I was, wearing bulky Snap Specs while facing the ground.

The Lens (what Snap calls apps on its augmented reality headset) is called Thirty Ups. It is in Halloween mode now, so when I look down, a virtual cartoon Jack-o’-lantern sits right next to where I’m supposed to start working out. I’m not trying to get jacked right now, but my goal is to see if these gigantic smart glasses will fall off when I’m staring straight down and moving up and down.

I get into position and start my workout. When I go down and back up, a little virtual circle on the ground below me starts counting up. I don’t get to 30 push-ups. I’m surrounded by people, many of whom are now staring at me, and it feels too hot outside to keep going without feeling gross. I get in 12 reps before giving up. The glasses only count 11 because it tells me I “skipped” one. Great.

The nearby Snap representative is thrilled. “You’re the first person who’s tried that one,” he says. I’m also pleasantly surprised. These glasses seem huge, but they stayed on my face just fine.

Snap announced its Specs in June. They cost $2,195 and will start to ship in the coming weeks. It took a few months for Snap to share what actual features would be available on the glasses

WIRED’s Julian Chokkattu and I both tried out Snap’s Specs last week. He got a dedicated demo with the company. I was offered one, too, but instead I happened to stumble upon the Specs First Look demo at the Westfield Century City shopping center in Los Angeles. The space has been here for just a couple of weeks.

It was a warm Sunday afternoon, and a steady stream of people came through the mall’s demo zone. Snap reps handed out Specs to anyone curious enough to register and hang out. Kids were running around, and the glasses looked especially large on their faces. When people left the demo, they got a free cup of ice cream with a small, Specs-shaped chocolate cookie.

The Specs had a dozen or so Lenses available for testing. Aside from the push-ups, the Specs let you finger paint in midair, see navigation directions overlaid on the real world, or engage with the physical environment by drawing on a notepad or analyzing text in a print book. They also have some sporty features, like one that allegedly helps with golf and another through a partnership with the NBA that guides you through shooting hoops.

You may have noticed that the glasses look pretty chunky. That’s true, but I was pleasantly surprised by how lightweight they felt and how well they stayed put. (The glasses come in two sizes, so if the small is too tight, try the larger model.) Another surprise was how well the virtual digital elements held up in bright light. I made a point of walking into direct sunlight to test out the screen. With the brightness turned all the way up, the onscreen elements were still visible. The glasses had automatically switched into “sunglasses mode” and dimmed to block the sun. The Snap rep said the lenses protect the eyes from UV rays at all times.

The problem, though, is that Snap is really trying to make the case that these glasses—or at least future, smaller iterations—are the holy grail of consumer tech. But I still don’t care to wear them in public. Walking around with the AR elements on can be distracting. Even if you turn it all off, the waveguides on the lenses still have a rainbow shimmer in your vision as you move. I wouldn’t want to wear these while driving or even walking when I really need to see where I'm going. At one point in the demo, I had to dodge a kid wearing a pair of Specs who was wildly swinging punches at something on the screen only he could see.

Most of the device features are controlled with your hands, like pinching two fingers together to open a lens or move something around. You can play Beat Saber-esque games by moving your hands around. But the controls can be finicky, and I found myself clawing at the air repeatedly to move or open something. Chokkattu tried writing in Google Docs—a demo showing the Specs as a computer you can work with anywhere—but the connected Bluetooth keyboard had a severe input lag, making typing a chore.

It also feels odd that some Specs features really just feel like advertising. A Harry Potter spell-casting experience is a fun idea, but really it just comes across as an ad for the upcoming HBO show. The Specs also have a shopping feature which lets you browse stores online. It’s a reminder that one day your augmented vision will be bombarded with pop-up ads.

I have a hard time imagining who these glasses are for. Given the price, it’s clearly aimed at developers and early adopters. But I tried the developer version of the Specs in 2024. The new glasses are much more comfortable and slightly less chonky, but the software hasn't changed much since then. Snap has shown off the same finger painting demo every time I’ve tried them, and every time it works until it doesn’t. The Specs are interesting but lack a killer feature, and Meta and Xreal both have more polished mixed-reality glasses that cost less. That’s going to make Specs a hard sell.

“We see consumer adoption as a process—the hardware, software, available experiences and price all need to develop together,” a Snap representative wrote in a statement to WIRED. “Specs bring computing into the world without pulling you out of it.”

For now, Snap’s most compelling pitch might be the free ice cream.

entries.title: I Gave My Blood to the AI Death Clock
entries.summary: Death Clock promises to predict when you’re going to die and help you extend your time on Earth. After a month, I felt like it was sucking the life out of me.
entries.content:
I am scheduled to die on August 10, 2060, at the age of 74.

So says my iPhone screen, where Death Clock, an AI-powered longevity app that predicts life expectancy based on your medical habits and lifestyle, has produced an image of a smiling grim reaper to celebrate my expiration date. There he was one September morning, looking especially thrilled about the reveal, gesturing with a peace sign as he reclined in a doughnut-shaped pool inflatable under that giant number: 74.

I have never resented getting older, but I suppose that’s younger than I’d like to be when my time is up. In the last four years—years that brought the passing of my grandmother and aunt within 18 months—I’ve become hyperaware of how finite my days are. Since turning 40 in January, I’ve also experienced daily reminders of aging: inexplicable pains that rotate between my back, neck, and hips. Spiritually, I feel young; physically, my body screams otherwise. Aging is natural, but I had a creeping suspicion I could buy myself more time.

Our collective obsession with life extension has given rise to a multitrillion-dollar longevity industry, bolstered by wannabe prophets like Bryan Johnson. Threats like climate change and AI doomerism only seem to have intensified existential fears, even as LLMs promise a new era of personalized medicine to address any health issue. Track enough pieces of data, the thinking goes, and algorithms can help you hack your own demise.

All of which led me to Death Clock, an app launched in 2024 aimed at tracking users’ health habits in an attempt to prolong their lives. In February, the company announced a new feature that lets you order biomarker panels. For a $69 subscription, you can get a basic blood panel that measures things like cholesterol, blood sugars, inflammation, vitamin D, and blood and organ health. There are also nine additional tests—assessing everything from hormones and micronutrients to your thyroid—that, altogether, cost $780. I opted for the routine blood panel and added the “stress” test ($29). Maybe some new insight could help me get a handle on it.

In an attempt to be more than another morbid countdown gimmick, Death Clock says it’s trained its AI on 1,200 longevity studies, actuarial data from life insurance companies, and life expectancy tables. Based on your results, its algorithms create a detailed prevention plan intended to help extend the time you have left.

Frankly, I was skeptical that anything meaningful would actually come from this. I was also, I can admit, a little fearful that I’d learn something I didn’t want to, a fact that might dissolve the little sanity I had left in a year that had already brought its share of unexpected problems.

After filling out an initial health questionnaire, a notification buzzed, forewarning my demise. There are three ways I will likely perish, it said: cardiovascular disease, a sleep disorder, or cancer (it doesn’t specify which type). This means, according to the app, I have already “completed” more than half of my existence on this mortal plane. A few days later, when I noted that my family has a mild history of diabetes, the app updated my age of death from 74 to 73.

And just like that, I lost a year.

I know I won’t live to be 100; people in my family generally croak in their early eighties. But was it possible to extend my lifespan by 10, even 15 years, with a hyperpersonalized plan? “You have two paths,” a message from the app exclaimed. “We are here to help you achieve the longer one.” I made an appointment with Quest Diagnostics, one of the two labs the company has partnered with, and willingly gave Death Clock my blood.

There’s no shortage of products that aim to reshape our relationship to our bodies. My inbox overflows with emails from longevity zealots pitching the latest anti-aging fads: salmon sperm scalp injections, a platelet-rich plasma treatment “Hailey Bieber swears by.” It’s almost too much, this urge to cheat the natural order of time.

“That’s a fool errand,” Death Clock CEO Brent Franson tells me one afternoon. He says advocates like Johnson—whose mantra “Don’t Die” reads more like a rejected Nike slogan than a wellness-oriented affirmation—“have to be really careful about inferring immortality when you have something to sell. That’s a dangerous place to be. The reality is we’re all going to die. It’s a question of when.”

Over Zoom, all I can think about is what Franson is trying to sell me.

The longevity market is projected to reach $8 trillion by 2030, meaning the future of health care may be shaped less by traditional treatment and more by personalized AI health services. With Doctronic, a HIPAA-compliant platform that works like a personal AI doctor, people can refill prescriptions without the need to see a human physician, while apps like Superpower and Lifeforce (similar to Death Clock) offer membership-based health insights and clinician-reviewed recommendations. Twin Health purports to create an AI replica, whatever that means, of a person’s metabolism. All of it is meant to help us live a little longer, though it’s unclear exactly how and at what cost.

Mike Ludkovski, a professor of statistics and applied probability at UC Santa Barbara whose research focuses on longevity analysis, says mortality awareness platforms like Death Clock “sell the illusion that individual lifespan is a linear process” that can be hacked. A 2024 Aging Cell study likewise suggested that an aging clock shouldn’t be treated as a measure of someone’s overall biological age. “Ultimately, individual-level triggers precipitating death are inherently random and will never be truly forecastable,” Ludkovski says.

I ask Franson if we’re actually getting healthier or just growing more anxious about being unhealthy. “I think both,” he says. “There’s a very unhealthy obsession with self-optimization—tracking everything, trying to control everything.”

Wasn’t Death Clock, in part, also guilty of that?

When the blood panels returned a week after I gave my sample, the results were mostly what my doctor had warned me about earlier this year. I’ve got borderline high cholesterol and blood sugar levels “creeping toward prediabetic range.” Shockingly, I have “optimal liver health” and normal cortisol levels. Videos from so-called wellness influencers had convinced me that a string of recent sleepless nights were the result of high cortisol, but, it turns out, the algorithm isn’t always right.

Based on my results, the app kept feeding me more tasks. Increase my vitamin D3! Schedule a DEXA scan for bone density! Discuss a prostate-specific antigen screening with a specialist! Despite Franson’s claim that he wants Death Clock to eventually be a replacement for primary care physicians, the app kept nudging me to discuss my results with a doctor.

Ultimately, I started to realize, tracking health data can only do so much. There is a belief, says Gretchen Terry-Leonard, author of Your Second Prime: Does Aging Suck, or Do We Suck at Aging?, that being able to measure something means it can also be managed. Death doesn’t work that way, she says, “so the measuring starts to serve a different need: the need to feel less afraid.”

Terry-Leonard is also the cofounder of the Center for Deeply Human Leadership, an independent research institute studying AI’s effect on brain health. She’s skeptical that consumer-facing longevity apps can lead to positive behavioral shifts on their own. “Facts don’t change minds,” she says. People understand that certain activities are unhealthy, but they do them anyway.

Keeping death in view is one of the oldest practices we have, and what seems to matter is whether a person feels they have the personal agency to make the necessary adjustments in their life. Researchers who study how thoughts of death shape health choices find that people move toward healthier behavior when they also have the confidence and resources to act, which not everyone does. “And without those,” Terry-Leonard tells me, “the anxiety tends to go into protecting how we feel about ourselves rather than into our health.”

While researching her book, Terry-Leonard found that older adults with more positive attitudes about aging lived an average of seven and a half years longer than those with negative outlooks. An app with a death countdown “can quietly teach us that aging is loss,” hindering longevity rather than promoting it.

In the month that I used Death Clock, this was the fact I couldn’t completely escape. I became a meticulous steward of my bodily functions, logging “daily habits” with the verve of an accountant manically calculating numbers just before tax deadline. In a single day I added 5.8 years to my life by earmarking that I’d completed at least 30 minutes of strength training, abstained from alcohol, brushed and flossed my teeth, gotten consistent sleep, spent time in the sauna, and drank more than eight glasses of water. But even as I labored to improve my death date, the clock was always there, counting down. It was an albatross that moved in a single, uniform direction: tick, tick, tick. Time became a burden I was being forced to optimize.

It makes sense that people are preoccupied with the very thing they are trying to escape. The need for control is addictive. But instead of assuaging my anxieties and questions about the great beyond, Death Clock only seemed to amplify them.

As the image of the life I want to build sharpens in my mind, a life that has already unfolded in deliciously unforeseen ways, I realize it has less to do with how I will make things happen and has everything to do with who I want them to happen with. Life isn’t about adding more time, but making it count when we can. I silenced Death Clock’s notifications on my phone and texted a friend: “Let’s meet at 7.”

Let us know what you think about this article. Submit a letter to the editor at [email protected].

entries.title: Reencle Essential Review: Same Scraps, Lower Price
entries.summary: Reencle has made your favorite kitchen composter cheaper—with a few compromises.
entries.content:
There’s a new Reencle composter in town, and of all the features I thought I might miss from the trailblazing original Reencle Prime, I didn't think it would be the auto-close lid.

The overly sensitive opening sensor annoyed me at first, but I ended up not giving the Prime’s lid another thought during my nearly 1.5 years of use. In hindsight, this is a testament to its convenience. It even has a setting for it to auto-open. Walk over to the receptacle, it opens; dump your scraps in, it closes. Buttons and lids remain clean and untouched by dirty, slimy hands.

Reencle’s brand-new, lower-cost unit, the Essential, is pretty much the same as the Prime (which is still available), with a few small tweaks—updated looks, a larger shovel, and a lid you have to manually close and a button you have to press to open. The button and lid already dirty after only three weeks, but my family consistently forgets to push the lid closed, having grown used to the auto-close lids of both our trash can and our old Prime. At least a few days a week, I will be caught off guard by a constant beeping—the Essential letting us know its lid is still open.

Aside from that, the Essential delivers the same user-friendly, close-to-compost-producing experience as its older sibling, but for $150 less.

Compost in Progress

You may have heard of kitchen composters before, whether the Lomi, FoodCycler, or the original Reencle Prime. It’s a compelling fantasy: Food scraps go in the bin, and out comes ready-to-use compost.

Unfortunately, for all of these machines, it’s just that: a fantasy. Many of them (like Lomi and FoodCycler) simply grind and dry the scraps to create a material that looks kind of like dirt. Sure, it’s odorless and shelf-stable, but if you want to use it in your garden, you’ll need to mix it into potting soil at a very low ratio—like 1:10, or even 1:20 if you’re processing a lot of meat and dairy.

Reencle, meanwhile, actually uses thermophilic bacteria (including Bacillus and Actinomycetes) to break down the waste, resulting in a biologically active material that, while not ready-to-use compost, is at least part of the way there. There are a couple of other machines that also do this, and I’ve tried them, but they’re bulkier, pricier, and louder than Reencle—don’t discount the noise-polluting effects of an audible fan running 24/7, especially if you live in a small space. (Reencle’s large-capacity Gravity model was—and remains—the only food recycler/composter I’ve ever tested that was truly silent at all times.)

entries.title: Law Firm Linked to Elon Musk Started an ‘Election Integrity’ Organization
entries.summary: The firm that helped set up Elon Musk’s America PAC is behind the new group, which will work with election officials to pursue policies aligned with Donald Trump’s false election fraud claims.
entries.content:
The law firm that helped set up Elon Musk’s America PAC has created a new, nationwide “election integrity” organization aligned with Donald Trump’s false claims of election fraud, WIRED has learned.

The organization, a nonprofit called the Association of State and Local Election Officials, was established by a lawyer then at Lex Politica, the Musk-linked law firm founded by Chris Gober, who was chief counsel for America PAC in 2024 and is now running in Texas for a spot in the House of Representatives.

The board of directors, according to the nonprofit’s registration filing in Texas, boasts Florida secretary of state Cord Byrd, current and former state election officials in Georgia, a Michigan state representative, and the president of Cleta Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network, a Trump administration-aligned election denial group. Byrd announced his involvement with the group—which he said won’t begin until after the election—alongside Florida governor Ron DeSantis in September, as the pair touted its mission, which aims to bring what they call “election integrity” policies down to the state and local level nationwide.

It’s not clear if Musk is involved in the organization. Until now, Musk has simply been a funder of Republican candidates and causes, and a benefactor of government contracts. Musk’s financial involvement in the midterm elections has been extensive: Musk’s America PAC is financing a sprawling canvassing operation aimed at helping Republican candidates get out the vote in November, and Musk is the single largest donor to Republican candidates this election cycle, spending more than $445 million, targeting Senate races key to maintaining a Republican majority. Since July, Musk has spent nearly as much money—$276 million—to boost Republican candidates as he did during the entire 2024 presidential election cycle. These elections are crucial for Musk. If Democrats win majorities in the House and Senate, Musk and his companies could be the subject of congressional investigations.

The link between a law firm that has worked with Musk and officials involved in purported “election integrity” activities is not surprising. For years, Musk has pushed the racist great replacement theory, which posits that minorities are systematically replacing white people in the US and in Western countries around the world. Election denialism—rooted in the unfounded theory of widespread voting by undocumented immigrants—is part of that racist theory of demographic societal change.

Musk has continually pushed election conspiracies that align with Trump’s false claims of election fraud, and this year, he’s doubled down. Musk has been a major disseminator of election misinformation this cycle, and recently boosted the false story that Texas US senate candidate James Talarico had been committed to a psychiatric facility in Ohio. America PAC has also spread inaccurate information about mail-in ballots.

The Association of State and Local Election Officials was first registered on June 17 by Michael Garcar as a nonprofit in Texas. At the time, Garcar was an attorney at Lex Politica, which was expanded after its lead lawyer, Gober, helped launch Musk’s America PAC. Gober has represented Musk’s and America PAC’s political interests in court cases in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

On July 20, the Association of State and Local Election Officials was granted tax-exempt status by the IRS, according to an agency letter addressed to the organization at its Washington, DC, address. That address—a box in a UPS Store on Pennsylvania Avenue—is the same as the one Garcar listed on the organization’s Texas filing and belongs to Lex Politica, according to a US Supreme Court filing from one of the firm’s attorneys, Erin Hawley, wife of Senator Josh Hawley. The nonprofit’s Texas registration was first unearthed by True North Research, a Democratic-linked research group.

Garcar has since left Lex Politica and now works for Five Rings Law Group. The firm lists just two partners—both Lex Politica alums—and former Koch Industries lawyer Jenny Kim. Before launching Five Rings, Kim worked for Gober.

Garcar, Kim, and Gober did not respond to questions about Lex Politica’s ties to the Association of State and Local Election Officials.

At a September 24 press conference about the organization, Byrd and DeSantis announced their partnership with the nonprofit and said the Association of State and Local Election Officials will use Florida’s hard-line voting and election rules as a “blueprint” to enact similar policies across the country.

Byrd said the organization would “have state chapters to support, educate, and train local and state election officials on election integrity, because that’s something that the other side has been very good at.”

“They’re the ones going in and certifying and training people who run our elections, and not doing it in a way that we think comports with the law and voter trust,” Byrd said. The association “will be a national organization to promote election integrity, principles, and federal law and policy,” he added.

Under Byrd and DeSantis’ leadership, Florida has enacted rules and laws that voting rights advocates have criticized, including passing a state version of the federal SAVE Act that requires proof of citizenship at polling locations and prohibits the use of student IDs to vote beginning in 2027. “I’m very excited to head up that initiative and take what we’ve done in Florida as the blueprint, as the model for the nation, take it nationwide,” Byrd said in September.

The offices of Byrd and DeSantis did not respond to questions about their involvement with the organization.

The organization’s board is also staffed by Sharon Bemis, the president of Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network, the country’s most prominent election denial organization; Julie Adams, an election denier who is both a member of the Fulton County Board of Elections in Georgia and a regional coordinator for the Election Integrity Network; Janice Johnston, who recently left the MAGA-dominated Georgia State Election Board; and Michigan state house representative Ann Bollin, who has coordinated with the Election Integrity Network.

The organization’s board members did not respond to questions for this story, though Johnston and Bollin have both previously denied being election deniers. The organization’s Texas registration contains no information about its work, and the group does not appear to have a web presence.

But the presence of Johnston and Adams on the board is telling.

In Georgia, Adams has made a name for herself by pushing Trump’s conspiracies about widespread election fraud and has sued multiple times for access to voting records with the help of the Republican National Committee. She has refused to certify results without being allowed to inspect voting records.

Johnston recently left Georgia’s State Election Board for what she said were “family and personal responsibility” reasons, and her time there was marked by turmoil, partisanship, and legal battles based on false fraud claims. Under her direction, the election board pursued specious investigations of Fulton County, supported mass voter purges championed by election denial activists, and worked to effectively eliminate voting machines.

Adams and Johnston have long targeted Fulton County for supposed fraud, and gleefully celebrated when, in January, the FBI raided an elections warehouse there, seizing tens of thousands of ballots from the 2020 election. Johnston was one of the unnamed witnesses in the FBI affidavit that preceded the raid, providing information about alleged double-counted ballots to the agency that had already been investigated and proven to have had no effect on the outcome of the 2020 election.

The Justice Department briefly fought in court to keep her name hidden from public view, but described a witness in the affidavit as “a Republican-appointed member” of the State Election Board who previously “was an obstetrician,” which identified Johnston. As the raid was being carried out, Johnston went live on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast from an SUV parked nearby.

When asked about Johnston’s presence on the board of the new Musk-linked election denial organization, Sara Tindall Ghazal, the lone Democrat on the Georgia State Election Board and Johnston’s former colleague, replied, “lol.”

“I mean this quite seriously, ‘lol.’ That’s my comment,” she tells WIRED.

And while Musk has quietly increased his political funding of Republicans, he has taken a bit of a step back from publicly discussing or posting about US politics and elections—with the exception of Talarico. His most recent post about voting is from September, when he responded to a question from Senator Mike Lee, a Republican from Utah. “Who benefits from noncitizen voting?” Lee asked on X.

“Democrats, which is why they push for open borders and noncitizen voting!” Musk responded. “Incentives explain behavior.”

entries.title: Liquid Glass Finally Makes Sense on the iPhone Duo
entries.summary: Liquid Glass was a divisive redesign. But with a radically different iPhone, the pieces are finally falling into place.
entries.content:
Apple rarely admits a mistake. But when it unveiled new versions of its operating systems this summer, it came close.

“With all major design updates, there’s a natural process where we take a bold leap forward, and then we continue to iterate,” said Apple's human interface designer, Shubham Kedia, during a predictably sleek keynote video. “Our team really appreciates your feedback, and we considered it deeply as we refined the new design.”

Not quite “Sorry, everyone, we messed up,” but for Apple, practically an apology tour. The subject was Liquid Glass, Apple’s most divisive interface design since at least iOS 7. Apple's Vision Pro mixed-reality headset (which itself flopped) inspired the translucent design language, and the company brought it to millions of other Apple devices.

The result was a mess—at odds with Steve Jobs’ famous line, “Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.” Liquid Glass started obsessed with gloss and effects, despite promises it would bring your content to the foreground. Yet Apple’s own press release showed interfaces with illegible text. Worse, users found constant reflections and flickering color shifts distracting, and a lack of clarity across devices hurt accessibility.

But iOS 27, alongside updates to Apple's other software platforms, signaled a shift in priorities after Kedia’s mea culpa. Kedia spoke of reincorporating design cornerstones in what was, if not quite a U-turn, then at least a rediscovery of a core principle: how it works. Instantly, interface elements across Apple devices gained greater clarity and structure, making it easier to tell apps' components from content. The most obvious change, though, was a slider.

Thinking Differently

Apple said it tuned Liquid Glass to diffuse complex content more effectively, keeping elements legible when above imagery and text. But it also acknowledged that not everyone wants the same thing—some users might prefer a more tinted look, and others “would like Liquid Glass to be even more clear.” You can now decide for yourself with the Liquid Design slider in Settings. For a company known for being opinionated, such bet-hedging was surprising but not unwelcome. Choice isn’t a bad thing, and now users had more of it.

“I immediately pushed that slider all the way to the most tinted setting, and pretty much all the legibility issues vanished,” Ben Rice McCarthy, an indie developer behind popular apps like Obscura and Indigo, tells WIRED. McCarthy has long criticized Liquid Glass. Now? Not so much.

“Liquid Glass introduced a lot of issues without adequate solutions, but this year’s operating systems solved or improved a lot of them,” McCarthy says. “There’s the adaptiveness of the interface. Buttons can grow into menus. Controls merge and divide like cells as you transition between views. Toolbars can expand and contract smoothly as the view changes size.”

Flexibility matters when resizing windows across any device. But while announcing its updates, Apple also dropped major hints that all but confirmed new hardware—it showed iPhone apps running on an iPad or a Mac could resize to a suspiciously specific shape that matched the rumored inner display dimensions of Apple’s upcoming folding phone.

Designed to Flow

When Apple showed off the iPhone Duo, everything clicked. Its passport-shaped display bucks the trend of iPhones and their rivals growing taller over the years. The Duo is wider and almost squat, and when opened, it naturally defaults to landscape, echoing the iPad Mini display.

Apple being Apple, it wanted to avoid the jarring jolt between displays that’s often evident on rival foldables, so it made content appear to move seamlessly from one screen to the other. That begins with the hardware. As Molly Anderson, Apple's vice president of Industrial Design, said at the September keynote: “To achieve this continuity, we designed iPhone Duo around a consistent aspect ratio that is the same across both displays.” But it’s the software—rooted in Liquid Glass—that sells the illusion.

The most arresting element is a fancy animation, which various folks in the Android space are now busy being “inspired” by. It reinforces the idea of a flowing interface. Meanwhile, Liquid Glass freed Apple from being prescriptive about where essential controls live. On the Duo, they sit at the side. When the phone’s closed, that frees up space for content. When it’s open, the controls stay in a consistent spot, so you never have to hunt for them. Reorient the device, and everything settles into the most appropriate place.

That’s form following function, not function being subservient to form. This device and its flexible interface don’t strictly need the Liquid Glass design language, but the two feel made for each other. Liquid Glass finally makes sense on the iPhone Duo—and with Apple’s other refinements, it’s starting to make sense elsewhere, too.

Clarity of Purpose

How much of this is happenstance is hard to say. Given Apple’s lead times, pure coincidence seems unlikely. And even if Liquid Glass wasn’t made with the Duo in mind, it adapts to it.

Liquid Glass feels more considered. It’s increasingly tuned for individual devices rather than governed by a “universal” aesthetic forced onto them all. The result is operating systems that feel solid rather than fragile, with interfaces less likely to fight content for your attention. On Macs and iPads, the Liquid Glass revamp now looks more like a love letter to Aqua—Apple's water-themed interface introduced in 2000. On the iPhone, it’s usable again. On the Duo, it’s a delight.

That’s not to say it’s perfect. “There’s some weirdness that hasn’t been fully resolved, and there needs to be a consistency to all these materials or the metaphors break down,” McCarthy says. “But overall, Liquid Glass is vastly improved.”

And it’s worth remembering that while the Duo is new, Liquid Glass is relatively young, too. As developer Steve Troughton-Smith wrote, “For some iPhone apps, even with keen developers, it will take six months to a year of work to properly support iPhone Duo. A lot of developers are still trying to finish the Liquid Glass transition they started last year.”

A useful reminder that transitions take time. But at least now, Apple’s vision looks clear.

entries.title: Astronomers Discover a Possible New Dwarf Planet in Our Solar System
entries.summary: Lying beyond Pluto, 2026 ED138 could be as large as 1,500 kilometers in diameter. Astronomers are still working to confirm whether it meets the criteria for a dwarf planet.
entries.content:
Scientists are on the verge of confirming the discovery of another member of the solar system, a potential dwarf planet. Astronomers at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile located the object, provisionally named 2026 ED138.

The prospective planet measures somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers in diameter and is located about 46 astronomical units from the sun (an astronomical unit being Earth’s approximate distance from the sun). For comparison, Pluto—which is also now considered a dwarf planet—orbits at an average distance of 40 astronomical units. Based on its location, ED138 belongs to the population of trans-Neptunian objects. According to its discoverers, it could be one of the brightest known objects of this type and also among the largest.

The difference between a planet and a dwarf planet is largely their environment. While both orbit the sun and have sufficient gravity to assume a nearly spherical shape, a planet has cleared its orbit of other bodies of comparable size. Dwarf planets, on the other hand, coexist with other objects in the region of the solar system they traverse. This is the main reason why Pluto ceased to be considered a planet in 2006 and was reclassified as a dwarf planet.

Matthew Holman, a researcher at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics and a member of the observatory’s operations team, identified the object on October 13 while analyzing data collected by Rubin in 2026. A more thorough search allowed the team to locate additional observations in archived records dating back to 2016. Thanks to this set of images, the team was able to reconstruct more than a decade of the object’s trajectory.

Astronomers explain that ED138 had managed to “hide” from us because its position in the night sky is against the disk of the Milky Way, which we usually see as a thick band of millions of stars. This concentrated brightness makes it difficult to distinguish fainter objects, but the Rubin Observatory’s enormous amounts of data made it possible to identify the object amid that sea of light.

Though ED138 appears to have the right characteristics, astronomers have yet to confirm whether it is a dwarf planet. For now, astronomers know it is a trans-Neptunian object, but they need to determine its size more precisely to establish whether its own gravity is sufficient to give it a nearly spherical shape. If it meets the requirements, ED138 would join the group of five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris.

It is also not the only celestial body awaiting possible classification as a dwarf planet. Astronomers have identified dozens of objects in the outer solar system that, based on their size and other characteristics, could meet the criteria. Among the best-known candidates are Gonggong, Quaoar, Sedna, and Orcus. Experts acknowledge that the list could be even longer.

Confirming them as dwarf planets is no easy task. The enormous distance at which they lie makes it difficult to directly measure their size and mass and, above all, to determine whether their own gravity has given them a nearly spherical shape. To obtain high-resolution images of Pluto, for example, the New Horizons probe had to be sent to its vicinity—a journey that took nearly nine and a half years from its launch in 2006 to its flyby in 2015. Three years later, it reached the object Arrokoth, a small planetesimal even farther away.

The solar system is often depicted as a star surrounded by eight planets, but in reality it is a much more extensive and populous structure. In addition to planets and moons, it contains dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, and a vast number of small bodies that extend far beyond Neptune. The Kuiper Belt extends to approximately 50 astronomical units, while the scattered disk reaches nearly 1,000. Much farther out lies the Oort Cloud, a region we have never directly observed and that could extend up to about 100,000 astronomical units from the sun.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.
